summary: After a series of September investor conferences hosted by major banks, the article concludes that global investors see Japan as "back" but need more persuasion that the revival will last. Prime minister Fumio Kishida is making his strongest push for investment this week as Larry Fink and other fund heads gather in Tokyo. Drivers include Tokyo Stock Exchange capital-efficiency pressure, Warren Buffett's investments, improved corporate governance, investors rotating away from China, and government reforms like the Nisa expansion.
one_line: Global investors are warming to Japan amid a stock rally, governance reform and China worries, as Kishida courts investment, though doubts about durability remain.
key_facts: In September, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Mizuho, BNP Paribas and Jefferies hosted investor conferences in Tokyo, New York, Hong Kong and London on whether Japan is really back.
Prime minister Fumio Kishida will make his strongest-ever push for investment this week as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other global fund heads gather in Tokyo.
Kishida told the Economic Club of New York: "I would urge you to evaluate what we are doing in my country... and then invest in Japan."
Topix, Japan's main stock index, has risen more than 25 per cent this year, outperforming almost all developed market indices, and the equity market is at a 33-year high.
Paul Hitchens of Jefferies cites the Tokyo Stock Exchange's push for better capital efficiency and Warren Buffett's heavy investment in five of Japan's largest trading houses as catalysts.
Keith Truelove of UBS Securities Japan says family offices and high net worth individuals show strong interest and there is still "a lot of dry powder on the sidelines".
Truelove notes Japan has offered investors many false dawns, so the bar for deciding 'this time is different' remains high.
Asia-focused global investment is rotating out of China into Tokyo stocks, real estate and other assets, helped by US-China tensions, chip wars, decoupling and "friendshoring".
China's slower growth, an elusive post-pandemic rebound and sudden crackdowns on industries like video games and private tutoring are eroding its appeal.
Kirk Neureiter of Fidelity says new Japanese CEOs took office after the 2014 stewardship code and 2015 corporate governance code and view their role differently.
Kishida has promised major reform of Japan's $5tn asset management industry to ease entry for foreign and new players.
The government plans to expand the Nisa tax-free investment scheme from next year to unlock $14tn in household financial assets held in cash and bank deposits.
Stefanie Drews of Nikko Asset Management says allocation to Japan used to be tactical but is now strategic.
